==Problem==

A classroom has a row of 35 coat hooks. Paulina likes coats to be equally spaced, so that there is the same number of empty hooks before the first coat, after the last coat, and between every coat and the next one. Suppose there is at least 1 coat and at least 1 empty hook. How many different numbers of coats can satisfy Paulina's pattern?

[[File:2025AMC8Prob22.png|center]]

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 2\qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 4\qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 5\qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 7\qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 9</imath>

==Solution 1==
Suppose there are <imath>c</imath> coats on the rack. Notice that there are <imath>c+1</imath> "gaps" formed by these coats, each of which must have the same number of empty spaces (say, <imath>k</imath>). Then the values <imath>k</imath> and <imath>c</imath> must satisfy <imath>c+k(c+1)=35 \implies kc+k+c=35</imath>. We now use [[Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick]] as follows: <cmath>kc+k+c=35</cmath> <cmath>\implies kc+k+c+1=36</cmath> <cmath>\implies (k+1)(c+1)=36</cmath> Our only restrictions now are that <imath>k>0 \implies k+1 > 1</imath> and <imath>c>0 \implies c+1>1</imath>. Other than that, each factor pair of <imath>36</imath> produces a valid solution <imath>(k,c)</imath>, which in turn uniquely determines an arrangement. Since <imath>36</imath> has <imath>9</imath> factors, our answer is <imath>9-2=\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~7}</imath>. ~cxsmi

==Solution 2==
Say Paulina placed <imath>n</imath> coats. That will divide the 35 hooks into <imath>n+1</imath> spaces and <imath>35-n</imath> empty hooks. Therefore, <cmath>n+1|35-n</cmath> The values of <imath>n</imath> that satisfy this are <cmath>n\in{1,2,3,5,8,11,17}</cmath>The answer is <imath>\boxed{\text{(D) }7}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
Let the number of empty hooks before the first coat be denoted as <imath>n</imath>.

This means that there are <imath>n</imath> empty hooks between all the coats. In every situation, there are <imath>n + 1</imath> gaps, since <imath>n</imath> cannot be zero.

To solve the problem, subtract <imath>2n</imath> from 35 (accounting for the <imath>n</imath> empty hooks at the beginning and <imath>n</imath> empty hooks at the end). Then subtract 1 (for the first occupied hook). After that, divide the remaining number of hooks by <imath>n + 1</imath> (the number of hooks between coats). We do this because the first occupied hook is always after <imath>n</imath> hooks; we just need to check if the remaining hooks can be evenly divided by the number of gaps.

To clarify: 

* If <imath>n = 1</imath>:
\begin{align*}
35 - 2n &= 33 \\
33 - 1 &= 32 \\
\frac{32}{n + 1} &= 16 
\end{align*}

Since 16 is an integer, this situation satisfies the conditions.

*If <imath>n = 2</imath>:
We can skip the the third step, as each time you add 1 to <imath>n</imath>, it decreases by 2 from the previous situation.

<cmath>\frac{30}{n + 1} = 16</cmath>

This situation also satisfies the conditions.

Continue this process until the difference exceeds <imath>35 - (2n + 1)</imath>. We find that 7 situations satisfy the conditions. Therefore, the answer is 7.

''Note: This method is slow but easy to check and understand.''


~LIBAIKO

==Solution 4 (Similar to Solution 1 but without Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick)==
Suppose there are <imath>n</imath> occupied hooks on the rack. Observe that there are <imath>n+1</imath> intervals, each of which must have the same number of empty hooks. Let's suppose <imath>m</imath> is the number of empty hooks plus the occupied hook to its right. Then, we have the equation <cmath>(n+1)m-1=35</cmath> <cmath>\implies (n+1)m=36</cmath> Our restrictions are n > 0 and m > 1. 36 has 9 factors, and two pairs do not meet the restriction. Our answer is then <imath>9-2=\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~7}</imath>.

~Brainwhizz

==Solution 5 (neat trick)==
Note that, for any possible valid arrangement of coats, there is always a set number of empty coat hangers between the coats. This is never 0, since then there would be no empty hangers on either side. So suppose there is <imath>n</imath> hangers between every coat. Then, there is one coat every n+1 hangers. For any value of <imath>n+1</imath>, divide it into 35, the amount of hangers. If <cmath>35/(n+1)</cmath> has a remainder of <imath>n</imath>, then that would be a valid arrangement for that value of <imath>n+1</imath>. This works for values of 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, and 18. This means there are <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~7}</imath> total possible arrangements.

-Arm123

==Solution 6 (fastest)==
Note that this simplifies to the amount of factors of 36, the total amount of places. This is 9, and take the factors 1 and 36 out to get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D)}~7}</imath> total possible arrangements

~ Devansh M
